**CHICAGO, Illinois (CNN)** — Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich declared Friday that he is innocent of federal corruption charges and vowed to fight the allegations, making his first public statement since his arrest earlier this month.

“I am not guilty,” Blagojevich told reporters outside his Chicago office. “I intend to stay on the job, and I will fight this thing every step of the way.”

“I will fight, I will fight, I will fight until I take my last breath,” he added.

Blagojevich was arrested December 9 after federal prosecutors accused him of attempting to use his office for personal and political gain. Among the allegations in a criminal complaint is that the governor sought something of value in exchange for appointing a successor to President-elect Barack Obama’s vacant U.S. Senate seat.

Prosecutors have said court-authorized recordings captured Blagojevich discussing the Senate appointment in profane terms and describing it as “a [expletive] valuable thing.”

The complaint also alleges that Blagojevich tried to pressure the owners of the *Chicago Tribune* to dismiss editorial writers who had criticized him, and that he sought campaign contributions in connection with official state action.

Blagojevich did not address the specific accusations Friday. He urged Illinois residents to reserve judgment and said he looked forward to proving his innocence.

The governor has faced mounting calls to resign from Democratic and Republican leaders in Illinois and Washington. State lawmakers also have begun considering impeachment proceedings.

Blagojevich’s attorney has said the governor’s recorded conversations have been taken out of context and that the defense will challenge the government’s case.

No replacement for Obama had been named at the time of Blagojevich’s statement. Under Illinois law, the governor held the authority to fill the vacancy, though state officials were exploring ways to strip him of that power or hold a special election.

**Blagojevich rejects resignation calls, refuses reporters’ questions amid Illinois political crisis**

*December 19, 2008*

**CHICAGO, Illinois (CNN)** — Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich vowed Friday to fight federal corruption charges but refused to answer reporters’ questions, deepening the political turmoil surrounding his administration and the vacant U.S. Senate seat once held by President-elect Barack Obama.

“I am not guilty,” Blagojevich said during a brief appearance in Chicago. “I will fight. I will fight. I will fight until I take my last breath.”

The Democratic governor left immediately after his statement, ignoring shouted questions about whether he would resign, how he could continue governing and whether he still intended to appoint Obama’s successor in the Senate.

Blagojevich’s public defiance came 10 days after FBI agents arrested him at his Chicago home. Federal prosecutors charged the governor and his chief of staff, John Harris, in a criminal complaint with conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud and solicitation of bribery. Harris later resigned.

Neither man had been convicted, and Blagojevich’s attorneys said the governor was entitled to the presumption of innocence.

### Allegations involving Obama’s Senate seat

The most explosive accusations concern Blagojevich’s authority to appoint someone to complete the final two years of Obama’s Senate term.

Federal prosecutors allege that Blagojevich treated the appointment as a political and financial commodity, discussing ways he and his wife might personally benefit in exchange for naming a particular candidate.

In secretly recorded conversations described in an FBI affidavit, the governor allegedly called the Senate seat “a valuable thing” and said he was unwilling to give it away “for nothing.” Prosecutors said he explored possible benefits including a high-paying job for himself, a position with a nonprofit organization or labor group, substantial campaign contributions and employment for his wife.

U.S. Attorney Patrick Fitzgerald said the allegations showed a “political corruption crime spree” and accused Blagojevich of putting a “for sale” sign on the Senate seat.

The complaint does not accuse Obama of wrongdoing. Fitzgerald said prosecutors were making no allegations against the president-elect, who resigned from the Senate after winning the November election. Obama has said he had no contact with Blagojevich about the appointment and has called on the governor to step down.

An internal review by Obama’s transition team was expected to detail contacts between members of the incoming administration and the governor’s office. Obama has said he is confident that no member of his staff discussed an improper deal.

### Broader corruption accusations

The federal complaint extends beyond the Senate vacancy.

Prosecutors allege that Blagojevich repeatedly sought campaign money or personal benefits in return for official state action. Among the accusations:

- **Children’s hospital funding:** Blagojevich allegedly threatened to withhold millions of dollars in state assistance for a children’s hospital unless its chief executive arranged a campaign contribution.
- **State contracts and legislation:** The governor allegedly pressured individuals and businesses seeking state action to provide political contributions.
- **The Chicago Tribune:** Prosecutors say Blagojevich discussed withholding state help connected to the sale of Wrigley Field unless the Tribune Company removed members of the *Chicago Tribune* editorial board who had criticized him and advocated his impeachment.
- **Personal employment:** The complaint says Blagojevich considered using his official authority to obtain a lucrative private-sector position or other financial security once he left office.

The allegations are based in part on court-authorized wiretaps and recordings made during a lengthy federal investigation of Illinois government.

Blagojevich has not provided detailed responses to the accusations. His legal team has indicated it will challenge the government’s interpretation of the recorded conversations and has warned against judging the case before all the evidence is presented.

### Bipartisan demands for resignation

Political leaders from both parties have said Blagojevich can no longer govern effectively.

Obama, Illinois’ other U.S. senator, Dick Durbin, and Senate Democratic leaders have urged him to resign. Illinois Attorney General Lisa Madigan, also a Democrat, asked the state Supreme Court to declare Blagojevich unable to serve, although the court declined to intervene.

Lt. Gov. Pat Quinn has said the governor should leave office and allow him to assume the governorship. State legislative leaders have also begun considering impeachment proceedings.

Republicans have joined the demands, arguing that the allegations have damaged public confidence and left major state decisions under a cloud.

The pressure has not persuaded Blagojevich to relinquish either his office or his power to fill the Senate vacancy. His continued refusal has raised the prospect of a prolonged constitutional and political confrontation.

### Senate appointment in doubt

The arrest created immediate uncertainty over how Illinois would fill Obama’s former seat.

Some lawmakers initially proposed changing state law to require a special election rather than allowing Blagojevich to make the appointment. Support for that approach later became entangled in partisan concerns about the cost of an election and the possibility that the seat could change parties.

National Senate leaders warned that any appointment made by Blagojevich could face serious questions about legitimacy. Democratic senators said a person selected under the circumstances might not be seated.

Legal experts noted, however, that Blagojevich remained governor unless he resigned, was removed through impeachment or was otherwise declared unable to serve. An arrest and criminal complaint alone do not automatically strip a governor of constitutional authority.

### Government under a cloud

The scandal has disrupted state business at a time when Illinois faces serious budget problems and rising unemployment. Lawmakers and agency officials must continue working with an administration whose leader is under federal investigation and facing possible removal.

The controversy also revived Illinois’ long history of political corruption. Blagojevich’s predecessor, former Republican Gov. George Ryan, was convicted on federal corruption charges and was serving a prison sentence when Blagojevich was arrested.

Blagojevich, who was elected in 2002 as a reformer and won a second term in 2006, had already been locked in bitter disputes with state legislators, including members of his own party. His strained relationship with Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan complicated efforts to address the state’s financial problems even before the federal case became public.

Now lawmakers must decide whether to move forward with impeachment while federal prosecutors prepare their criminal case. The Illinois House has established a committee to examine whether there are grounds to impeach the governor. If the House approves articles of impeachment, the state Senate would conduct a trial and determine whether to remove him.

For the moment, Blagojevich remains in office and insists he will be vindicated. But by refusing to resign—or to answer questions about the conduct described in the federal complaint—he has left Illinois facing an extraordinary struggle over who can govern, who can speak for the state and who should fill one of its two seats in the U.S. Senate.
